newsitem.title: USA: Smut blockers, adult sites prepare for life after CDA.
newsitem.headline: Smut blockers, adult sites prepare for life after CDA.

text.p: X-rated Web sites and publishers of the smut-filtering software that block them obviously don't have much in common. One exception: for each, it's been business as usual since the Supreme Court's decision overturning the Communications Decency Act.

In the weeks immediately following the June 26 decision, when the nation's highest court upheld an earlier ruling overturning parts of the controversial act as unconstitutional, neither side has detected a significant surge in demand.
But in the long run, both operators of adult Web sites and publishers of filtering software expect to gain from the decision.

"I think we'll see an increase in traffic because it brings attention to us and anything that brings attention" brings business, said Barbara Bailey, co-owner of Cyber Sex World, a Las Vegas company that runs the Pleasuregirls.com and Babetime.com Web sites.

From opposing vantage points, both parties also believe parents must do more to control how their families use the Internet now that the courts have issued their hands-off directive to federal regulators.

"The trick is to get parents to use it," said Sydney Rubin, a spokeswoman for Microsystems Software Inc., of Framingham, Mass., publisher of CyberPatrol and a party to a lawsuit challenging the CDA that led to the Supreme Court's ruling.

"Parents are a little intimidated by computers until they take the time to actually use them," Rubin said. "But once they do, they discover using filtering software is about as simple as clicking a mouse."

Though short-term demand for filtering products hasn't increased, publishers say growth is going nowhere but up. Programmes such as CyberPatrol (http://www.cyberpatrol.com), SurfWatch (http://www.surfwatch.com), NetNanny (http://www.netnanny.com) and CyberSitter (http://www.cybersitter.com) allow an adult to block childrens' access to Web sites, Usenet newsgroups, chat rooms and other areas on the Internet or online services they deem to contain sexually explicit images, violent language or otherwise unacceptable material.

Since filtering software came on the market two years ago, consumers have bought millions of programmes and downloaded millions of other copies for free from online services such as America Online Inc. and CompuServe Corp.

Coinciding with the Supreme Court decision, publishers are turning out new versions of the software they claim are easier to use, offer more individualized controls, and in some cases, make it more difficult for a determined teenager to hack into the password mom or dad uses to set filter codes.

For example, an upcoming version of NetNanny, from NetNanny Software International in Vancouver, British Columbia, will incorporate a technology called keystroke dynamics that identifies a person based on the rhythm of their keyboard typing.

"When you set up a password using keystroke dynamics it creates an electronic signature. If you enter a password, (the program) will reject it if the dynamics aren't right," said Net Nanny President Gordon Ross.
Net Nanny expects to have a demo of the new software on their Web site next month, and will incorporate it in a forthcoming version for corporate Internet users called NN Pro, Ross said.

The just-released SurfWatch 3.0 blocks 40,000 Web sites and allows parents to block access to Web-based chat rooms and Internet relay chat, which the company maintains are popular areas for pedophiles and other predators. A "manager" feature allows parents to turn off controls to view sites that otherwise would be blocked.

Microsystems Software expects to deliver an upgraded version of CyberPatrol next month that comes with a simplified default setting for parents new to computers or, for old hands, more elaborate controls for adjusting privacy settings.

In another new feature Microsystems demonstrated at a Federal Trade Commission hearing last month in Washington, parents will be able to control the level of privacy they prefer for each child in a family and block access to Web sites that collect information on children for marketing and promotional purposes.
Such controls are a great idea, said Cyber Sex World's Barbara Bailey.

"I have grandchildren and a lot of computers around the house and I have (filtering software) on them so the kids can't see anything I don't want them to see," Bailey said. "You don't leave Playboy laying around on the coffee table, you have blocking on TV so you can block out the adult channels. It's the same for the computer."

According to Bailey, Cyber Sex World goes to great lengths to prevent minors from logging onto the company's adult sites. On the other hand, in these post-CDA days, Cyber Sex World and other adult sites like it are making themselves as attractive as possible to potential customers. The company's new Babetime.com site, for example, charges $49.99 a day for customers to view live strip shows and other sexual fare. That's a steep drop from the $4.95 to $5.95 per minute customers pay at Pleasuregirls.com, the company's other Web site.
"It's more affordable for everyone," Bailey said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
